title: Hidden in a cave
hookLine: four big questions, and the answer Hindus still use when the texts disagree: walk where the great have walked
carry: dharma is hidden; walk where the great walked

lines: WHAT IS THE PATH? WHAT IS THE NEWS?
cards: Four more questions, and they're the big ones. The yaksha has asked about the sun and the earth, about friends and anger and greed. Now he asks four in a row.
Who is happy? What is wonderful? What is the path?
And what is the news? Four brothers are still lying on the shore. The answers have to be true, not clever, and Yudhishthira gives each one in a sentence or two.

teach.h: HAPPY: GREENS AT HOME, AND NO DEBTS.
teach.b: Who is happy? Yudhishthira's answer is wonderfully small. The person who cooks simple greens in their own home, late in the day, who owes nothing to anyone, and doesn't have to live away from home.
Hear that from a prince in exile. What is the news? The world is a great cooking pot.

teach.h: THE NEWS: TIME COOKS EVERY CREATURE.
teach.b: Time is the cook, with the sun for fire and days and nights for fuel, stirring every creature with the months and seasons for a ladle. What is wonderful?

teach.h: THE WONDER: WE LIVE AS IF WE WON'T DIE.
teach.b: Every day, living beings go to the house of Death, and those who are left live as if they never will. And what is the path? Here he's honest about how hard it is.
Argument doesn't settle it. The scriptures say different things. There isn't one sage whose view everyone accepts.
The truth of dharma is hidden as if in a cave.

teach.h: THE PATH: WHERE THE GREAT HAVE WALKED.
teach.b: So the path is the one the great have walked. That answer is a big Hindu teaching. Hinduism has no single book or pope to settle every question.

The old law books name the Vedas and tradition as sources of dharma, and beside them, the conduct of good people. So when the texts seem to disagree, Hindus look to how the wise and good actually live.
The week began with Savitri talking with Death on the road. It ends with a brother talking with a stranger at a lake. In both, the one who speaks truly about dharma saves the others.

how: On the path, Yudhishthira concedes that argument is unsettled and the scriptures differ, and points to the way the great have gone; Hindu law books likewise count the conduct of good people as a source of dharma.

o: a fixed rule written once for everyone
the reward that comes after a good deed
the right way, hidden as if in a cave

games.q: four big answers — tap the pairs.
p: the one the great have walked
we live as if we won't die

s: Yudhishthira said the path is found by winning the argument
he said argument doesn't settle it and the scriptures differ, so follow the path the great have walked.
in his answer, happiness is a simple meal at home with no debts
and not having to live away from home.
the wonder, he said, is the sun rising each day
it's that people see others die every day and still live as if they never will.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. the yaksha asks: what is the path? you know the scriptures differ and arguments go in circles. what do you answer?
o: the one the great have walked.
games.why: the truth of dharma is hidden as if in a cave, he says, so the path is the one the great have walked.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose life shows you dharma: a grandparent, a teacher, someone quietly good. Let their face come clear.

Now think of one choice in front of you this week, and ask, without arguing it out, what would they do? Breathe with that answer for a few breaths. If you pray, ask for the courage to walk where they walked.

wordCard.voice: Dharma, the right way, hidden as if in a cave, Yudhishthira says, so we follow the path the great have walked. Supper at home, time stirring the pot, and the wonder that we live as if we never die. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Yudhishthira's answer: the path is the one by which the great have gone.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma is hidden; walk where the great walked. Greens, a home, and a path someone good has already worn. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), the episode of the Yaksha's questions: the last four questions (who is happy, what is wonderful, what is the path, what is the news)
Sources of dharma in the dharmashastra: Veda, smriti (tradition) and the conduct of the good (Manusmriti 2.6, 2.12, in general)
